claims.text: The initial automotive alloy catalyst contains Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt in roughly equal proportions.
ALD can deposit a trace, approximately 0.1 nm Pd layer on the multi-principal-element alloy surface.
Annealing at approximately 150 °C after ALD will stabilize the deposited Pd dispersion.
The deposition and annealing treatment will form stable Pd–Cu interfacial ensembles.
The Pd dispersion will self-adjust during redox cycling.
The stabilization treatment will prevent Pd agglomeration during redox cycling.
Cu provides the ability to oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at low temperatures.
Pd provides resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
Pd–Cu interfacial synergy will enhance CO and hydrocarbon oxidation below 150 °C.
The modified catalyst will resist activity loss during transient H2O and NO exposure better than the unmodified catalyst.
Suppressing Pd sintering or agglomeration will preserve catalytic activity over extended cyclic aging.
The modified catalyst will have greater long-term durability than the unmodified catalyst.
Adding the sub-monolayer Pd treatment will keep overall platinum-group-metal usage minimal.
The unmodified near-equiatomic catalyst has limited low-temperature oxidation performance.
The unmodified catalyst is unstable under redox cycling and is prone to sintering and high-mileage degradation.
The intervention will remain effective during automotive temperature cycling, redox cycling, H2O and NO exposure, and accelerated high-mileage aging.
Thermal spikes beyond normal automotive operation may limit the intervention's effectiveness.

contradictions.description: A roughly equiatomic Cu–Ni–Pd–Pt alloy would contain about 50 at.% platinum-group metals before modification. Calling the resulting catalyst low-PGM or claiming that adding Pd keeps overall PGM usage minimal is inconsistent unless low use is defined on a mass, surface-loading, or support-normalized basis.
